title: Prefix Caching and RadixAttention: How Modern LLM Engines Reuse KV Caches Across Multi-Turn Chats and Agent Workflows
summary: In conversational AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic loops, large language models repeatedly process overlapping prompt prefixes—such as system instructions, retrieved documents, or multi-turn chat histories. In standard serving architectures, the engine recomputes Key-Value (KV) tensors for the entire context on every single turn, bottlenecking GPU compute during the prefill phase and causing painful Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) delays. RadixAttention and automatic prefix caching solve this by organizing GPU KV memory as a dynamic Radix Tree (compact trie), matching token prefixes in constant time, reusing cached KV tensors directly in High Bandwidth Memory, and evicting cold branches via Least Recently Used (LRU) policies. This slashes multi-turn prefill times by up to 90% and triples serving throughput without modifying model weights.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Master Chef's Mise en Place Tree vs. Re-Chopping Soup Bases From Scratch
analogy:
Imagine running a high-volume restaurant specializing in artisan ramen and noodle soups. Every bowl ordered starts with the exact same 4-hour simmering bone broth and base mirepoix (onions, carrots, celery).

If your kitchen operated like a traditional naive LLM engine, whenever a customer ordered 'Spicy Miso Ramen with extra pork', the line cook would pull out raw whole carrots, whole onions, and raw bones, spend 45 minutes dicing and boiling the broth from absolute zero, just to add the final scoop of miso paste and sliced pork at the very end. When the customer asks for a side dish or refills ten minutes later (Turn 2), the chef tosses everything in the garbage and chops all the raw vegetables all over again from scratch!

RadixAttention operates like a master kitchen with an organized mise en place holding station. In the center of the kitchen sits a heated tree of pre-prepped bases: Trunk A is the master golden broth. Branch B splits into chicken stock; Branch C splits into vegan dashi. When an order arrives, the chef looks at the ticket, matches the longest common prefix on the prep counter ('Ah, golden broth + miso base already hot on burner #3!'), scoops out the pre-heated base in two seconds flat, and only cooks the unique requested toppings (the new turn's prompt tokens). When the kitchen runs low on counter space (GPU VRAM), the kitchen porter clears away the Least Recently Used (LRU) specialty sauces that haven't been ordered all evening, keeping popular common bases instantly available.

sections.heading: 1. The Multi-Turn Bottleneck: Why Recomputing Common Prefixes Stalls GPU Prefill
sections.content:
In production LLM applications, modern workflows are dominated by repeated context. Consider three ubiquitous patterns:
• Multi-turn Conversations: In a 10-turn conversation, Turn 10 contains all prompt and response tokens from Turns 1 through 9. Without caching, the engine reprocesses all historical tokens again from scratch.
• Few-Shot Prompting and RAG: Applications prepend a large 2,000-word system prompt or a 5,000-token enterprise knowledge base to hundreds of concurrent user questions.
• Agentic Reasoning Loops: Frameworks like DSPy, AutoGen, and tool-calling agents generate multiple reasoning branches and self-correction iterations off a single shared task description.

During the initial prefill phase of LLM execution, the GPU runs parallel matrix multiplications across all input prompt tokens to compute the Query ($Q$), Key ($K$), and Value ($V$) activations. While computing attention across $N$ tokens has an arithmetic cost of $O(N^2)$, repeating this computation when 90% of the tokens have already been evaluated in the previous turn wastes vast amounts of GPU Tensor Core compute and memory bandwidth.

Naive caching systems attempt to match prompt strings using hash tables. However, exact string hashes break down instantly when system prompts are shared across different users, or when conversations fork into different branches. What LLM engines need is a structure capable of matching arbitrary common prefixes across disparate requests at the granular token level.

sections.heading: 2. Radix Trees in GPU Memory: How RadixAttention Tracks and Shares Tensors
sections.content:
To solve prefix matching without rigid hash tables, modern inference frameworks such as SGLang introduced RadixAttention, an architecture now adopted in systems like vLLM (Automatic Prefix Caching).

Instead of tying KV cache allocations to isolated request lifecycles, the engine maintains a global Radix Tree (compact trie) over all token sequences resident in GPU High Bandwidth Memory (HBM):
1. Nodes and Edges: Each edge in the Radix Tree represents a sequence of token IDs. Each node holds pointers to physical GPU memory pages (managed via PagedAttention) that store the exact Key and Value projection matrices for those tokens.
2. Constant-Time Prefix Traversal: When a new prompt arrives, the engine tokenizes the string and walks down the Radix Tree from the root, matching token IDs sequentially. The traversal stops at the deepest node that matches the prompt's prefix.
3. Instant Cache Hit: If the first 3,500 tokens of a 4,000-token prompt match an existing branch in the tree, the engine instantly maps those 3,500 token KV cache pages into the new request's logical page table. The GPU Tensor Cores completely skip prefill calculations for those 3,500 tokens, computing activations only for the remaining 500 suffix tokens.

This changes the initial Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) from 1,800 milliseconds down to under 50 milliseconds, as the engine transforms a heavy matrix multiplication problem into a lightweight pointer lookup.

sections.heading: 3. Cache Eviction, Forking, and Cache-Aware Request Scheduling
sections.content:
Maintaining KV caches in GPU memory introduces a critical resource challenge: GPU VRAM is strictly finite. When memory is full, how does the engine make room for incoming requests without thrashing?

• Reference Counting & LRU Eviction: Every node in the Radix Tree maintains a reference counter indicating how many currently executing inference requests depend on its KV blocks. When a request finishes generating tokens, the reference counters along its path decrement to zero. However, instead of immediately freeing the memory pages, the engine retains the tree nodes and marks them as unreferenced. If free memory runs low, a Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction policy purges the oldest unreferenced leaf nodes first, freeing physical pages while preserving hot shared roots (such as the base system prompt).
• Branch Forking for Speculative Agents: When an agent evaluates multiple potential solutions in parallel (e.g., Tree-of-Thought search or majority voting), each branch forks off the common parent node in the Radix Tree. All worker threads share the exact same physical KV cache pages for the parent prompt, consuming zero duplicate VRAM.
• Cache-Aware Request Routing: In multi-GPU clusters, intelligent load balancers route incoming user requests to the specific worker node that already holds the matching prefix in its local VRAM. This maximizes cluster-wide cache hit rates and eliminates redundant cold-start prefills across worker pools.

takeaway: Recomputing Key-Value projections for identical system prompts, document contexts, and chat histories wastes massive GPU compute and causes high first-token latency in multi-turn applications. RadixAttention and automatic prefix caching solve this by treating GPU KV memory as a dynamic Radix Tree, matching token prefixes in constant time and skipping redundant matrix multiplications. By combining instant prefix lookup with LRU eviction and cache-aware request scheduling, modern LLM serving engines slash Time-To-First-Token by up to 90% and massively expand concurrent serving capacity.
